title: Judgments and Models
coreMove: Use a statistical model as the reference floor before deciding how much human adjustment to layer on top, rather than treating the model as a check on human judgment after the fact.
sourcePressure: Statistical models are consistent: they have no occasion noise, no between-model variation, and no pattern drift. Research consistently shows that simple linear models outperform expert clinical and professional judgment in many prediction tasks — not because models are brilliant but because they are consistent. The expert's value is in setting up the model correctly and in handling genuinely novel cases that fall outside the model's training range.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating model use as a threat to expert autonomy or as relevant only in high-volume data-processing contexts, rather than as a baseline that should inform any prediction before human adjustment is added.

sourceAnchors.name: Paul Meehl and actuarial vs. clinical judgment research
sourceAnchors.detail: Paul Meehl's landmark 1954 work and subsequent meta-analyses showed that simple actuarial formulas consistently outperform clinical judgment in prediction tasks, and that adding expert override to model outputs typically reduces rather than improves predictive accuracy — because overrides introduce inconsistency (noise) without adding useful information.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Paul Meehl called it the 'broken-leg problem': if you have a model that predicts movie attendance and you hear that the subject has a broken leg, you override the model. That override is sensible. Most overrides are not. Most overrides are noise in a suit.

hook: robots are better at predicting than humans
your gut is lying to you about predictions
counterintuition: an algorithm beats an expert almost every time
models don't need experts — experts need models
tryThisNow: build a simple scoring model for your next hire decision
compare your last ten predictions to a baseline rule
examples: a scene where a model-only decision is shown to be clearly better than human judgment — this collapses the nuanced message that models are better on average, not always
a scene where the model fails catastrophically in a specific case — that is the exception rather than the rule

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: Model-vs.-judgment examples risk all reading as 'model wins.' The examples must show the range of interactions — model as baseline, override dynamics, the broken-leg exception, model construction as the expert's real value-add — to give an honest picture.

exampleSpecs.domain: actuarial vs. clinical parole risk assessment: a parole board comparing model-only decisions versus officer-overridden decisions on a two-year outcome lookback
exampleSpecs.audience: a corrections department research team studying whether parole officer overrides improve or hurt recidivism prediction accuracy
exampleSpecs.stakes: public safety and prisoner rehabilitation — overrides that reduce accuracy relative to the actuarial tool are increasing both wrongful incarceration and undetected risk
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the research team presents the two-year outcome analysis: in the 200 cases where parole officers overrode the actuarial tool in the direction of greater leniency, the recidivism rate was 24 percent — 8 points above the tool's 16 percent for the same risk-score band; in the 80 cases where officers overrode toward greater restriction, the difference was smaller and not statistically significant; on average, overrides reduced accuracy
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a two-year outcome comparison chart showing recidivism rates by decision type: tool-only, lenient-override, restrictive-override — the lenient-override bar noticeably taller than the tool-only bar
mustInclude: the 24 vs. 16 percent gap for lenient overrides
the smaller gap for restrictive overrides
the research team's framing: the overrides are adding noise, not insight — they introduce inconsistency without improving the information basis
mustAvoid: implying parole officers should not exercise any judgment

exampleSpecs.domain: college admissions holistic review: a university comparing the predictive validity of formula-based admission scores versus admissions officer holistic assessment
exampleSpecs.audience: a university admissions research team studying which input better predicts four-year graduation and GPA
exampleSpecs.stakes: admissions quality and educational equity — if holistic assessment adds noise without adding signal, the students admitted through officer judgment graduate at lower rates
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the research team reviews five years of outcomes: the formula score (standardized academic indicators combined into a composite) predicts 4-year GPA with a correlation of 0.44; the admissions officer holistic assessment predicts with a correlation of 0.31; and in the sample of students admitted by holistic override of formula rejection, 4-year completion rates are 7 percent lower than the formula-admitted population at the same score range
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a two-predictor accuracy comparison table: formula composite in one row, holistic assessment in the other, outcome correlations in the final column
mustInclude: the 7 percent lower completion rate for formula-override admits
the framing: this does not mean holistic assessment adds nothing; it means it adds noise faster than it adds signal in the aggregate
mustAvoid: a specific student or application story
implying admissions should be purely algorithmic without human review

exampleSpecs.domain: clinical diagnosis with algorithmic support: a hospital comparing diagnostic accuracy and consistency between physician-only, algorithm-only, and physician-with-algorithm workflows
exampleSpecs.audience: a hospital quality team studying the effect of diagnostic algorithm integration on physician accuracy and variance
exampleSpecs.stakes: diagnostic accuracy and consistent care — if the algorithm floor raises median accuracy, its integration has clear value even if top physicians perform better alone
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: two hospital quality leads present the three-way comparison: algorithm-only has the lowest variance and the second-highest accuracy; physician-only has the highest variance and the highest peak accuracy but lowest median; physician-with-algorithm as baseline has the highest median accuracy and reduced variance — the clinical director's takeaway is that the algorithm should set the floor, not replace the ceiling
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a three-panel box-plot comparison on a whiteboard: algorithm-only (tight, moderate), physician-only (wide, variable), physician-with-algorithm baseline (tighter than physician, higher than algorithm)
mustInclude: the physician-with-algorithm condition outperforming both others on median accuracy
the mechanism: the algorithm removes the worst physician decisions (noise floor), the physician adds value at the high end (genuine outliers and novel cases)
mustAvoid: implying physicians should only use algorithms

exampleSpecs.domain: fraud detection: a fintech company comparing algorithmic flag rates versus analyst review override rates for the same transaction set
exampleSpecs.audience: a fraud operations manager measuring whether analyst overrides of algorithmic flags improve detection accuracy
exampleSpecs.stakes: fraud losses and customer false-positive rates — analyst overrides that release fraudulent transactions or flag legitimate ones both have direct costs
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the manager asks: across the last 12 months, when analysts overrode the algorithm's fraud flag in the direction of release, what was the subsequent fraud rate on those transactions compared to the algorithm's predicted risk? The answer: analysts who released high-confidence algorithm flags had a fraud rate 3.2 times higher than the algorithm's false-positive rate — meaning analyst releases on high-confidence flags were adding noise, not expertise
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a fraud rate comparison table: algorithm-flagged transactions that were released by analyst override in one row, algorithm-flagged transactions that proceeded to investigation in another — fraud rates visible in the right column
mustInclude: the 3.2x fraud rate in analyst-released transactions versus algorithm false positives
the high-confidence flag specification (not borderline flags — those are exactly where analyst expertise matters)
the manager's proposed policy: analyst overrides allowed only for borderline flags, not high-confidence ones
mustAvoid: implying fraud analysts add no value — the point is that overrides on high-confidence flags add noise, not that analyst judgment is universally valueless

exampleSpecs.domain: surgical scheduling: a hospital comparing model-predicted surgery duration versus surgeon-estimated duration for scheduling accuracy
exampleSpecs.audience: a hospital OR scheduling manager studying over- and under-booking patterns
exampleSpecs.stakes: OR utilization and patient care — systematically over-booked ORs produce overtime costs; under-booked ORs produce wasted capacity; surgeon-estimate variance drives scheduling noise
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: you compare two scheduling approaches: surgeon self-estimated duration has a mean absolute error of 23 minutes and a standard deviation of 31 minutes; the model-predicted duration (based on procedure type, patient factors, and surgeon historical data) has a mean absolute error of 18 minutes and a standard deviation of 12 minutes — and the surgeons with the largest estimation errors are also the surgeons who most resist using the model estimate as a starting point
exampleSpecs.firstImage: two scheduling accuracy summaries for the same OR suite: surgeon-estimated durations in one column, model-predicted durations in another, actual durations in a third — the model column tracking closer to actuals
mustInclude: the 23 vs. 18 minute mean absolute error and the 31 vs. 12 minute standard deviation
the higher resistance from surgeons with the largest errors
the framing: using the model as a starting point does not eliminate surgeon input; it eliminates the surgeon's idiosyncratic over-confidence in estimating duration
mustAvoid: a surgical delay patient harm story
implying surgeons have no useful information to add to scheduling

exampleSpecs.domain: real-estate automated valuation versus appraiser override: a bank comparing model-only versus appraiser-adjusted valuations on a portfolio of residential properties
exampleSpecs.audience: a bank lending quality officer studying whether appraiser adjustments to automated model values improve or hurt loan portfolio quality
exampleSpecs.stakes: lending risk management — appraisers who inflate above the automated value expose the bank to greater collateral risk; appraisers who deflate below suppress creditworthy lending
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the quality officer presents the three-year portfolio analysis: appraiser adjustments above the automated valuation model correlated with higher subsequent default-adjusted-LTV losses; appraiser adjustments below the automated value showed no significant difference from model-only decisions; the largest upward adjustments were made by a subset of appraisers and explained by client-relationship factors rather than property characteristics
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a scatter plot of appraiser adjustment magnitude on the x-axis versus subsequent default-adjusted-LTV loss on the y-axis — a positive slope visible only for upward adjustments
mustInclude: the client-relationship explanation for the worst upward adjusters as a noise source, not a quality signal

skillTargets: explain why models outperform expert judgment on average in prediction domains where feedback is available
identify the conditions under which expert override of a model is likely to add value versus add noise
apply the model-as-baseline principle to design a human-model workflow for a described prediction task
analyze why experts resist models even when models outperform them on average
evaluate whether a described model-override policy would preserve the value of human judgment while reducing its noise contribution

tryThisNowSpec: For your next prediction decision — project risk, hire quality, revenue estimate — build the simplest possible scoring rule: pick the two or three case features that research suggests predict the outcome best, weight them, compute a score. Make your judgment, then look at what the score says. If your judgment is consistently above or below the score, you are overriding in one direction. If you are above sometimes and below other times, you are adding noise. Both are signals worth knowing.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one short paragraph (3 sentences) on why model consistency beats human peak performance when the population level matters, at least one 5+ sentence paragraph on the Meehl finding and why it has been consistently replicated, at least one one-sentence punch line about what 'human override' adds most of the time
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph on the broken-leg exception — the one case where override is clearly correct — to make clear that the argument is about average overrides, not about every override being wrong
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
